UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                     BEFORE THE
                       FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

                                                            )
Northern Indiana Public Service                             )
Company LLC                                                 )
                                                            )
         v.                                                 )                             Docket No. EL26-36-000
                                                            )
Midcontinent Independent System                             )
   Operator, Inc.                                           )
                                                            )

                            MOTION TO INTERVENE AND PROTEST OF
                             THE MICHIGAN ATTORNEY GENERAL

         Pursuant to Rules 211 and 214 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (“FERC”
or the “Commission”) Rules of Practice and Procedure, 1 Michigan Attorney General Dana
Nessel, on behalf of the people of the State of Michigan, seeks to intervene as a party in the
docket and submits this protest in response to the complaint filed by Northern Indiana Public
Service Company LLC (“NIPSCO” or the “Company”) requesting the Commission require
adoption of a cost recovery mechanism for costs to comply with the Department of Energy
Order 2 issued pursuant to Section 202(c) of Federal Power Act (FPA) to prevent the scheduled
retirement of NIPSCO’s R.M. Schahfer Generating Station Units 17 and 18 (the “Schahfer
Units”).

    I.   MOTION TO INTERVENE

         The Michigan Attorney General, 3 on behalf of the people of the State of Michigan, moves
to intervene in this proceeding. The People of the State of Michigan have a direct interest in the
outcome of this proceeding as the households and businesses of Michigan, along with the State



1
         18 C.F.R. § 385.211 (2025).
2
         Department of Energy Order No. 202-25-3 (May 23, 2025) (the “DOE Order”).
3
          See MCL 14.28 (“The attorney general . . . may, when in [her] own judgment the interests of the state
require it, intervene in and appear for the people of this state in any other court or tribunal, in any cause or matter,
civil or criminal, in which the people of this state may be a party or interested.”). See also, In re Certified Question,
465 Mich 537, 543-545, 638 N.W.2d 409 (2002); See also, Gremore v. Peoples Community Hospital Authority, 8
Mich. App. 56, 153 N.W.2d 377 (1967); See also, People v. O’Hara, 278 Mich. 281, 270 N.W. 298 (1936).

                                                            1
 itself, may face higher electricity bills as a result of the cost recovery mechanism at issue in the
proceeding.

    II.    SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT

           The Michigan Attorney General requests that the Commission deny the complaint,
because the underlying DOE Order justifying cost recovery is ultra vires, and, absent a valid
legal obligation to operate pursuant to FPA Section 202(c), the imposition of the costs of
operating the Schahfer Units on ratepayers pursuant to FPA Sections 205 or 206: (i) is not just
and reasonable and is unduly discriminatory or preferential; and (ii) violates the filed rate
doctrine. If the Commission is not inclined to deny the Complaint on the merits, the
Commission should instead use the discretion afforded by FPA Section 202(c) to dismiss the
complaint without prejudice until the scope and legal validity of the DOE Order is settled.

           If the Commission does not reject NIPSCO’s request, the Commission must, at minimum,
require that the cost recovery mechanism incorporate certain customer safeguards, including
provisions to facilitate a refund of the unlawful charges to customers (in the event the DOE
Order is invalidated) and to limit recovery to only those costs that are necessary to operate under
the limits imposed by the DOE Order (in the event the DOE Order is not invalidated).
Additionally, in order to comply with cost causation principles, the Commission must require
cost allocation on a load ratio share basis across the MISO region. The DOE Order asserts an
obligation under federal law to make the Schahfer Units available to operate on the basis of a
purported region-wide emergency, not local conditions, and accordingly any “benefit” of such
operation accrues region-wide.

    III.   PROTEST
           a. The Commission should deny NIPSCO’s Complaint because the DOE Order is
              ultra vires and the cost recovery mechanism is unnecessary—and unjust,
              unreasonable and unduly discriminatory—absent a valid FPA 202(c) order.

           NIPSCO requests imposition of its proposed cost recovery mechanism primarily on the
basis of FPA Sections 202(c), 306, and 309. 4 However, NIPSCO itself does not allege that
keeping the Schahfer Units available and operating them during the period of the Order is
necessary for resource adequacy or reliability. Indeed, NIPSCO’s Complaint acknowledges that

4
           NIPSCO’s Complaint at 1.

                                                  2
 MISO studied the Schahfer Units pursuant to its Attachment Y process, under which MISO
would have determined that retirement of the units would not result in violations of applicable
reliability criteria. 5 NIPSCO’s Complaint also acknowledges that such retirement was approved
through Indiana’s state-regulated Integrated Resource Plan (IRP) processes. 6 Further
emphasizing the soundness of the MISO and state-level resource adequacy planning, the most
recent North American Electricity Reliability Corporation’s (“NERC’s”) 2025-2026 Winter
Reliability Assessment identifies MISO as a “normal risk” for the winter months, the lowest
category of risk designation. 7 The 2025-2026 Winter Reliability Assessment also finds that
MISO’s anticipated and projected resources exceed the reference margin level. 8 Because
substantial evidence shows that the NIPSCO Units are not necessary to ensure reliable operation
during the period of the DOE Order, in MISO Zones 1-7 or elsewhere, forcing MISO customers
to bear the costs of the Schahfer Units’ operation is not just and reasonable.

         Cost recovery here under Sections 205/206 of the FPA would also violate the filed rate
doctrine. 9 NIPSCO has filed its complaint precisely because the MISO tariff does not permit
cost recovery for the costs it has incurred to make the Schahfer Units available to operate. If the
DOE Order is struck down by the courts, the Commission would have no choice but to refund
any charges to MISO’s customers because even “the Commission itself has no power to alter a
rate retroactively.” 10


5
         See, NIPSCO Complaint at 8 (“After performing its reliability analysis, MISO approved the Attachment Y
for both Units 17 and 18, effective December 31, 2025.”).
6
        See, id. (“Pursuant to its commitments in the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission approved settlement
agreements in Cause Nos. 45772 (August 2, 2023) and 46120 (June 26, 2025), NIPSCO intended to convert those
suspensions into retirements.”).
7
         North American Electric Reliability Corporation, 2025-2026 Winter Reliability Assessment (November
2025), https://www.nerc.com/globalassets/our-work/assessments/nerc_wra_2025.pdf, at 6 fig. 1.
8
         See, id. at 42 fig. 4. The reference margin level varies by region; it is used by system planners to quantify
the amount of reserve capacity in the system above the forecasted peak demand that is needed to ensure sufficient
supply to meet peak loads.” Id. at 41. MISO’s reference margin level is substantially higher than that of any other
region in North America. See, id. at 42.
9
           Old Dominion Elec. Coop. v. FERC, 892 F.3d 1223, 1226 (D.C. Cir. 2018) (“The Act also empowers the
Commission to fix or change rates and charges, but only prospectively. 16 U.S.C. § 824e(a). When a utility wishes
to alter the rates it charges, it must provide sixty-days’ notice to the Commission and file new rate schedules “stating
plainly the change or changes to be made in the schedule or schedules then in force and the time when the change or
changes will go into effect.” Id. § 824d(d).”).
10
         Arkansas Louisiana Gas Co. v. Hall, 453 U.S. 571, 578 (1981).

                                                           3
         The Commission’s authority to impose these retroactive and unjust and unreasonable
costs on MISO customers therefore hinges solely on the validity of the DOE Order. But the
DOE Order is ultra vires. Crucially, no evidence substantiates the DOE Order’s determination
that the MISO region faces an emergency during the period of the DOE Order. As discussed
above, NERC’s most recent winter 2025-2026 assessment plainly contradicts any assertion of an
emergency during the period of the DOE Order, and instead reinforces the soundness of the
MISO and state-level processes for planning the Schahfer Units’ retirement. Likewise, the
relevant grid operator (here, MISO) has not requested this DOE Order as necessary. The DOE
Order instead demonstrates an attempt by DOE to illegally and arbitrarily usurp the decided roles
of the state and grid operator here in resource adequacy planning. The Michigan Attorney
General further notes that the time-period for filing interventions and requests-for-rehearing on
the DOE Order has yet to run, and it is likely that rehearing on the DOE Order will be sought in
that context (with the potential for further litigation following the time-period for rehearing). If
DOE grants rehearing, the scope of operation of the Schafer units and, correspondingly,
NIPSCO’s costs to comply with the DOE Order, may change materially.

        The Commission should thus deny NIPSCO’s complaint. If the Commission is not
inclined to deny the complaint on its merits, it should use the discretion afforded by FPA Section
202(c)—which makes clear that issuing an order to prescribe compensation or reimbursement is
discretionary, not mandatory, and sets no timeline in which such matters must be resolved 11—to
deny the Complaint without prejudice as prematurely filed. Given that the DOE Order is invalid,
and the potential that the Department of Energy may change the scope of cost recovery on
rehearing, the Commission has good cause to defer its determination of a just and reasonable cost
recovery mechanism until these issues concerning the scope and validity of the DOE Order are
resolved. A delay is appropriate as a safeguard against the potential imposition of unjust and
unreasonable charges, and to avoid administrative inefficiency that would result if the DOE
Order changes in scope or is invalidated, necessitating refunds.




11
        FPA Section 202(c)(1) (“the Commission, after hearing held either before or after such order takes effect,
may prescribe by supplemental order such terms as it finds to be just and reasonable, including the compensation or
reimbursement which should be paid to or by any such party”) (emphasis added).

                                                         4
         b. If the Commission does not deny the Complaint, it must impose certain limits on
           the cost recovery mechanism in order to ensure just and reasonable
           compensation.

        If the Commission grants the complaint, the Commission must modify NIPSCO’s
proposed cost recovery mechanism to ensure any charges pursuant to it are just and reasonable.
Even when acting under Section 202(c), the Commission is only empowered to prescribe
compensation or reimbursement “it finds to be just and reasonable.” 12 NIPSCO’s proposed
Schedule 13 omits certain safeguards to limit cost recovery to only costs that are needed to operate
consistent with the DOE Order, and therefore risks violating longstanding Commission cost
causation requirements.

        Cost causation principles require that all rates must reflect to some degree the costs
actually caused by the customers who pay them. 14 Assuming arguendo that the DOE Order is
valid, customers are only responsible for the expenditures that are necessary to operate the
Schahfer Units for the limited period of operation set forth in the DOE Order and under the
conditions imposed (“economic dispatch” so as “to minimize costs to ratepayers” 15) by the DOE
Order; that is the scope of operation that the DOE Order deems necessary to address the
purported emergency, and circumscribes the scope of “benefits” of operation that customers are
responsible to pay for. In the context of SSR units or the comparable “Reliability-Must-Run”
(RMR) units in other RTO/ISO regions, the Commission has recognized, for example, that if a
generation resource recovers from load the costs of significant upgrades during the term of the
SSR or RMR Agreement, but then rescinds the suspension notice or otherwise returns to service,
such expenditures must be reimbursed to comply with cost causation principles. 16 Absent a
protective measure such as a clawback provision, the Commission has held that an SSR or RMR


12
        FPA Section 202(c)(1).
13
        NIPSCO Complaint, Attachment B.
14
          Constellation Mystic Power, LLC v. FERC, 45 F.4th 1028, 1051 (D.C. Cir., 2022); Pub. Serv. Comm'n of
Wisconsin, 150 FERC ¶ 61,104, 61,704 (2015) (“SSR cost allocation should be commensurate with reliability
benefits received from continued operation of an SSR Unit”).
15
        DOE Order No. 202-25-12 at 5.
16
         Midcontinent Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., 161 FERC ¶ 61,059 at P 55 (2017) (rejecting an interpretation of a
clawback provision in an SSR Agreement that “would potentially allow SSR owners to recover the total cost for
repair expenses that provide significant benefits beyond the term of the SSR Agreement”); Constellation Mystic
Power, LLC, 172 FERC ¶ 61,045, 61,420 at P 25 (2020).

                                                         5
 unit may unjustly and unreasonably receive a windfall if it forces customers to pay for
expenditures that enable the unit to later return to commercial operation. 17

        For the same reasons, any cost recovery mechanism applicable to the Schahfer Units
must include safeguards to limit the scope of cost recovery to only those expenditures necessary
for its limited scope of operation under the DOE Order and/or provide a clawback provision to
reimburse customers for all or a portion of costs if the Schahfer Units continue to operate beyond
the terms of the DOE Order. For example, extensive repairs, such as those that may extend
beyond the period of the DOE Order, to render one of the Schahfer Units operational, 18 would be
inconsistent with the DOE Order. Such costs would not be necessary to ensure operation of the
units during the period of the DOE Order, and accordingly such costs would not be recoverable.
On this basis, NIPSCO cannot reasonably recover at least the following expenses:

                 a. Delivered cost of consumables inventory on-hand after the end of the period
                      of the DOE Order, including fuel and various materials used in environmental
                      control systems;
                 b. Costs of commodities or equipment to support continued operations that will
                      not be delivered until after the end of the period of the DOE Order.
                 c. Costs of maintenance or repairs that require generating unit shutdown past the
                      end of the period of the DOE Order; and
                 d. Costs of maintenance and repairs other than those strictly necessary to
                      maintain the operational status of the Schahfer Units until the end of the
                      period of the DOE Order.

        In addition, the DOE Order requires that MISO “take every step to employ economic
dispatch” of the Schahfer Units in order “to minimize cost to ratepayers.” While the DOE Order
lacks a precise definition of “economic dispatch,” a reasonable interpretation of this requirement
must give meaning to the directive to minimize costs to ratepayers. Any form of commitment
and dispatch that enables the Schahfer Units to operate at a net loss in their market operations,

17
         Midcontinent Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., 161 FERC ¶ 61,059 at P 55; see also Constellation Mystic Power,
LLC v. FERC, 45 F.4th at 1050-52 (rejecting as inconsistent with cost causation the Commission’s failure to justify
allocation of certain operating costs through the cost-of-service mechanism, where confronted with claims that those
expenditures also benefitted other customers).
18
         See, NIPSCO Complaint at 10 (referencing “investments that will be needed to bring Unit 18 back into
operation following an extended outage”).

                                                         6
 given their operating limits, is inconsistent with the DOE Order. 19 If NIPSCO self-commits the
Schahfer Units as “Must Run” units and the resulting dispatch results in a net loss in its market
operations over a period of time in which the plant could have been turned off (because it was
committed as Economic or Emergency), that operation resulting in a net loss cannot constitute
“economic dispatch” that “minimizes costs to ratepayers” as required by the DOE Order. 20
Likewise, if costs of repair are necessary to be operable, those costs must be factored in as a cost
of commitment. 21 The operation of the Schahfer Units can only qualify as “economic dispatch”
if the net energy value in market operations before the end of the period of the DOE Order
exceeds the cost of commitment including the necessary repairs. 22

        NIPSCO’s proposed MISO tariff schedule does not include any language to limit the
scope of recoverable costs to those that are necessary to comply with the DOE Order. The
Commission must direct MISO to incorporate such limits on cost recovery and incorporate other
safeguards, such as a clawback provision, to ensure the mechanism is just and reasonable.

        Finally, the most significant risk that the cost recovery mechanism will impose unjust and
unreasonable costs on customers is the likelihood that the DOE Order is overturned by the
courts. A just and reasonable cost recovery mechanism would facilitate reimbursement of
unlawful retroactive and unjust and unreasonable charges in the event the DOE Order is
overturned. 23

        c. To be consistent with cost-causation principles, cost allocation must be RTO-
           wide.

        NIPSCO proposes cost allocation to MISO Zones 1-7, premised on an assertion that this
reflects the scope and nature of the emergency addressed by the DOE Order. 24 However, it is

19
       See as explained in the Motion to Intervene and Protest of the Michigan Attorney General in FERC Docket
No. EL25-90-000, Affidavit of Douglas Jester at PP 10-17.
20
        See, id.
21
        See, id.
22
        See, id.
23
            The Commission’s experience with overseeing the refund of costs related to the Z2 process under SPP’s
tariff is illustrative. Unwinding retroactive charges can be tremendously complex and administratively burdensome
for the RTO/ISO. A tariff mechanism to track and reimburse charges could greatly reduce complexity and burden.
See generally SPP, “Attachment Z2 Status Report” at
http://spp.org/documents/72880/z2%20status%20update%2012.16.24.pdf
24
        NIPSCO Complaint at 6.

                                                        7
 incorrect to say that the DOE Order purported to identify reliability risks only in MISO’s northern
and central zones as the basis for the emergency. Any cost allocation must thus be on a load ratio
basis across the entire MISO region in order to meet cost-causation principles.

        The language of the DOE Order asserts an emergency throughout the entirety of MISO, 25
and it does not limit its assessment of the emergency to particular zones in MISO. The DOE
Order’s only reference to the Northern and Central regions specifically is in the context of the
MISO PRA Auction Results for Planning Year 2025-26. 26 However, Slide 4 of the same
document states that the North/Central zones have a higher effective summer margin at 10.1%
compared to the South zones at 8.7%. 27 To the extent that the DOE Order would be read to
establish that an emergency exists at all, that emergency would extend across the MISO region,
and would not be limited to any particular MISO zones.

        Moreover, assuming arguendo the validity of the DOE Order, then the operation of the
Schahfer Units would be necessary to comply with a federal law. Accordingly, the “benefit” of its
operation accrues broadly throughout the region. Under Commission precedent, cost allocation is
roughly commensurate with the benefits where the costs to comply with a law are shared across
the law’s applicable jurisdiction. For example, where New York State law required investment in
certain transmission infrastructure to achieve State policy objectives, the Commission held that it
is consistent with cost causation principles to allocate the costs of those projects on a volumetric
load-ratio share basis across New York State. 28 Following this precedent, the costs of complying
with the DOE Order must be allocated to the whole of the MISO region.




25
       See, e.g., DOE Order No. 202-25-12 at 2 (asserting a “resource adequacy emergency in MISO,” as
compared to MISO North and Central zones specifically).
26
       See, id.
27
          MISO, Planning Resource Auction: Results for Planning Year 2025-26, at 4 (April 2025),
https://cdn.misoenergy.org/2025%20PRA%20Results%20Posting%2020250529_Corrections694160.pdf.
28
        New York Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc. Niagara Mohawk Power Corp., 184 FERC ¶ 61,059 at P 47 (2023);
Consol. Edison Co. of New York, Inc. et al., 180 FERC ¶ 61,106, 61,739 at P 50 (2022).



                                                     8
 IV.    CONCLUSION

       For the foregoing reasons, the Michigan Attorney General requests that the Commission
deny NIPSCO’s Complaint, with or without prejudice. In the alternative, the Michigan Attorney
General requests that the Commission direct MISO to incorporate changes to the cost recovery
mechanism as discussed above.
